## Paper

## Abstract

Genome-wide association studies have identified 1p36.23 as a schizophrenia risk locus. However, the functional variants and genes driving the association remain unknown. Here, we identified two functional variants (i.e., rs159961 and rs301792) at the 1p36.23 risk locus. Both variants reside in introns of RERE and exhibit allele-specific enhancer activity. Risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 increase enhancer activity by altering REST and POLR2A binding, leading to RERE upregulation. Consistently, RERE was significantly elevated in brains of schizophrenia cases. Functionally, RERE-overexpression impaired neurogenesis, altered dendritic spine density and dendritic complexity, and altered genes related to dendrite development and glutamatergic synapses. Through interacting with RARB and RXRA at the Grin2a promoter, RERE regulates the well-known schizophrenia risk gene Grin2a (encodes an NMDA receptor subunit), and RERE-overexpression impairs excitatory synaptic transmission. Our study indicates that functional variants rs159961 and rs301792 confer schizophrenia risk by upregulating RERE, which affects neuronal development and synaptic function.

---

## Introduction

Schizophrenia (SCZ) is a severe and heterogeneous psychiatric disorder that affects approximately 1% of the global population. Due to its high prevalence, mortality, and morbidity, SCZ imposes a substantial economic burden and ranks among the top ten causes of disability worldwide. Unfortunately, the etiology of SCZ remains incompletely elucidated. Accumulating evidence indicates that genetic factors play a major role in the development of the disease. The heritability of SCZ is about 81%, underscoring the major contribution of genetic factors. So far, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified more than 300 SCZ risk loci. However, translating these genetic findings into insights regarding the underlying pathomechanisms remains a major challenge. Identifying potential causal variants and genes (or variants and genes with functional consequences) from risk loci is the first step toward a mechanistic understanding of disease biology. However, this step is hampered by the linkage disequilibrium (LD) among risk variants and the complex gene regulation process. As each risk locus usually contains hundreds or thousands of risk variants that show high-level LD, prioritizing causal variants from risk loci is a daunting task. Besides, even if the causal variant has been pinpointed, identifying the target gene affected by the causal variant is difficult, as many genetic variants regulate the expression of distal genes rather than genes located nearest to the risk variants. Thus, there is a pressing need to identify functional (or potential causal) variants from the reported risk loci.

To prioritize potential functional or causal variants from SCZ risk loci, we previously applied a functional genomics approach and identified 132 functional (i.e., affecting transcription factor binding) single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Among them, two functional SNPs (i.e., rs159961 and rs301792) on chromosome 1p36.23 showed robust associations with SCZ. These two functional variants reside in the intronic regions of RERE, a gene which was prioritized as the credible causal gene underlying 1p36.23 through fine-mapping, and affect the binding of transcription factors (TFs) REST and POLR2A. Although our functional genomics study has prioritized these two functional variants as likely causal variants at the 1p36.23 risk locus, the mechanisms by which they confer SCZ risk remain unknown. Specifically, the molecular mechanisms of their regulatory effects, the identity of their target gene, and the role of this gene in SCZ pathogenesis remain to be clarified.

In this study, we first demonstrated the regulatory mechanisms of the two variants with dual-luciferase reporter gene assays and electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA). We then identified RERE as the target gene regulated by these variants through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) analysis, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout assays, and TF knockdown assays, among others. Finally, we showed that RERE plays a critical role in regulating neurogenesis, dendritic spine morphogenesis, dendritic complexity, the expression of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor subunit GluN2A, and excitatory synaptic transmission. Our study identified likely causal variants and genes at the 1p36.23 risk locus and elucidated their underlying mechanisms in SCZ. These findings translate GWAS results into disease biology and provide important insights into the pathogenesis of SCZ.

---

## Results

rs159961 and rs301792 are functional SNPs at the 1p36.23 risk locus
GWAS have shown that 1p36.23 is a robust risk locus for SCZ. To pinpoint the likely causal variants from this locus, we previously used a functional genomics approach to identify functional (i.e., TF binding-affecting) SNPs. Our functional genomics approach showed that rs159961 and rs301792 are functional variants at the 1p36.23 risk locus. To further explore whether rs159961 and rs301792 are potential causal variants, we performed fine-mapping using SuSiE, CARMA, and FINEMAP. Genetic associations from populations of European-ancestry were used as input, and the results indicated the presence of an independent causal signal at this locus. SuSiE analysis yielded a 95% credible set that includes 55 SNPs. CARMA fine-mapping identified 102 SNPs, which comprise the 99% credible set. The 92% credible set comprised 50 variants in FINEMAP analysis. Notably, both rs301792 and rs159961 were included in the credible sets in all three analyses, with low posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) (rs301792 (PIP of SuSiE: 0.0073, CARMA: 0.0052, FINEMAP: 0.0066) and rs159961 (PIP of SuSiE: 0.0066, CARMA: 0.0046, FINEMAP: 0.0058)). The full results of the fine-mapping are provided in supplementary material (Supplementary Data 1–4).

SNPs rs159961 and rs301792 showed strong associations with SCZ in European populations. These associations were confirmed in both East Asian populations (29,519 cases, 44,392 controls) and cross-ancestry populations (96,806 cases and 492,818 controls) in our replication study, with the same risk alleles as in Europeans. These results indicate that these two variants are credible risk variants for SCZ. Both rs159961 and rs301792 are located in the intronic regions of RERE, and the intronic sequences containing rs159961 and rs301792 show enrichment for REST and POLR2A binding motifs. To validate the functionality of these two SNPs, we examined whether these two SNPs are located in active regulatory elements. Epigenomic data indicated that rs159961 and rs301792 are located in open chromatin regions (as detected by DNase-seq) that were marked with enhancer-associated histone modifications (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K9ac) in human neuronal cells and human brain tissues. To further assess the functional consequences of rs159961 and rs301792, we conducted dual-luciferase reporter gene assays. Both risk alleles (rs159961-T and rs301792-G) exhibited increased enhancer activity in SH-SY5Y cells (a human neuroblastoma cell line) compared with protective alleles (rs159961-C and rs301792-A). In U251 cells (a human glioblastoma cell line), the rs159961-T allele also exhibited higher enhancer activity than the C allele, whereas rs301792 alleles showed no significant difference. Notably, the allele-specific enhancer effects were absent in HEK-293T cells, indicating the regulatory effects of these variants are neuronal-dependent. Collectively, these results support the regulatory effects of these two functional variants.

Molecular regulatory mechanisms of rs159961 and rs301792
Our reporter gene assays revealed the neuronal-dependent regulatory effects of rs159961 and rs301792. To dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying these neuronal-dependent regulatory effects, we conducted EMSA. The EMSA showed that different alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 affect the binding affinity of TFs. The super-shift assay indicated that rs159961 binds to REST, as a super-shift band was observed when REST antibody was added. The risk allele (T allele) of rs159961 attenuated binding to REST compared with the protective allele (C allele). Different alleles of rs301792 also exhibited differential binding to POLR2A, as the binding intensity was decreased when POLR2A antibody was added. The risk allele (G allele) of rs301792 demonstrated stronger binding ability to POLR2A compared with the A allele. Takentogether, these results indicate that functional genetic variants rs159961 and rs301792 regulate the enhancer activity by affecting the binding affinity of REST and POLR2A, respectively.

Risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 confer SCZ risk by upregulating RERE expression
To further identify the target gene(s) regulated by these two functional variants, we examined their associations with gene expression in the human brain. The largest brain eQTL dataset, BrainMeta (v2), which was generated using human brain tissues, was explored. Both rs159961 and rs301792 showed significant associations with the expression of RERE (P=1.39×10⁻⁴⁸ and P=1.98×10⁻⁴⁹), RERE-AS1 (P=4.56×10⁻⁸ and P=4.72×10⁻⁸), and SLC45A1 (P=1.51×10⁻⁴ and P=1.64×10⁻⁴). The strongest associations were observed for RERE, suggesting that these two functional genetic variants may confer SCZ risk by regulating RERE expression. In addition, eQTL analysis using postmortem adult brain tissues also showed that the risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 were associated with higher expression of RERE, consistent with the results of reporter gene assays. To test the colocalization posterior probability (PP) between the 1p36.23 locus and the eQTLs for RERE, we conducted colocalization analysis. The results showed that the colocalization PP of the 1p36.23 locus with the eQTLs for RERE was high (0.854), supporting that genetic variants in this locus confer SCZ risk by regulating RERE expression. However, we noticed that the colocalization PP for SNP rs159961 and rs301792 was relatively low, SNP.PP.H4=0.09 for rs301792, and SNP.PP.H4=0.013 for rs159961. These consistent results suggest that risk alleles of these two functional variants contribute to SCZ risk by upregulating RERE expression.

To further investigate whether rs159961 and rs301792 regulate RERE expression, we performed CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing. We knocked out ~300bp genomic sequences encompassing the rs159961 or rs301792 sites, followed by quantification of RERE expression. The real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) results showed that deletion of these genomic regions led to downregulation of RERE, indicating that the genomic elements containing rs159961 and rs301792 function as enhancers to regulate RERE expression. In addition to RERE, rs159961 and rs301792 were also associated with SLC45A1 expression (P=1.51×10⁻⁴ and P=1.64×10⁻⁴). However, these associations were much weaker than those with RERE (P=1.39×10⁻⁴⁸ and P=1.98×10⁻⁴⁹). We further examined whether knockout of rs159961 or rs301792 affected SLC45A1 expression. The results showed that the rs159961 knockout significantly downregulated SLC45A1, but the rs301792 knockout had no significant effect. Together, these results suggest that RERE (rather than SLC45A1) is the main target gene regulated by these two functional variants.

To investigate whether rs159961 and rs301792 regulate RERE expression independently or synergistically, we performed conditional eQTL analyses and haplotype analyses. Conditional eQTL modeling indicated that rs159961 and rs301792 exert non-independent effects on RERE expression. Haplotype analysis further revealed that only the AC/GT diplotype (heterozygous combinations of both risk alleles) was significantly associated with increased RERE expression, suggesting a potential synergistic regulatory effect. rs159961 and rs301792 affect the binding of REST and POLR2A, implying that these two variants interact with REST and POLR2A to regulate RERE expression. We thus knocked down REST and POLR2A in SH-SY5Y cells using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs). REST and POLR2A knockdown resulted in significant down-regulation of RERE. Furthermore, Pearson’s correlation analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between REST and RERE expression in the human brain. Collectively, these results indicate that these two TFs interact with rs159961 and rs301792 to regulate RERE expression.

rs159961 and rs301792 are located in intronic regions of RERE, suggesting that they may regulate RERE expression through long-range interactions. Hence, we examined whether the genomic regions containing rs159961 and rs301792 interact with the promoter region of RERE, using Hi-C data. Hi-C data showed long-range interactions between the genomic regions containing these two functional variants, and the RERE promoter in human hippocampus. Together, these results indicate that the risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 upregulate RERE expression by affecting the binding of REST and POLR2A.

TWAS supports RERE as a SCZ risk gene
The above data suggest that RERE is the likely causal gene regulated by rs159961 and rs301792. To further validate this, we performed a transcriptome-wide association analysis (TWAS) by integrating eQTL data from postmortem adult brain tissues (from the PsychENCODE project) and SCZ GWAS. This analysis identified 234 genes that showed significant associations with SCZ risk. Notably, the TWAS supported that RERE is a SCZ risk gene whose genetically predicted upregulation is associated with SCZ risk (Z-score=6.24, P=4.46×10⁻¹⁰). The TWAS result is consistent with the reporter gene assays and eQTL data, which showed that the risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 were associated with higher RERE expression. The TWAS results provide robust support for the involvement of RERE in SCZ.

RERE was significantly upregulated in the brains of SCZ cases compared with controls
TWAS and eQTL analysis suggested that functional risk variants confer SCZ risk by upregulating RERE. If this conjecture is true, RERE expression should be higher in SCZ cases than in controls. To further test whether RERE upregulation is associated with increased SCZ risk, we examined RERE expression in the brains of SCZ cases and controls. Consistent with eQTL and TWAS results, RERE expression was significantly upregulated in the brains of SCZ cases compared with controls (P=8.45×10⁻⁹). The significant upregulation of RERE in SCZ cases compared with controls provided further evidence supporting that functional risk alleles confer SCZ risk by upregulating RERE expression.

RERE affects the proliferation and differentiation of mNSCs
Our consistent and convergent results suggest that risk alleles of rs159961 and rs301792 upregulate RERE expression, which in turn contributes to SCZ susceptibility. To explore the potential role of RERE in SCZ pathophysiology, we examined its function in neurodevelopment using the NSC model, which is widely used in delineating SCZ pathogenesis. We first examined RERE expression in major cell types in the human and mouse brain. The results showed that RERE was broadly expressed, with relatively higher expression levels in neurons and astrocytes, implying that this gene may have a role in neurodevelopment. The proliferation and differentiation of NSCs are crucial for brain development, and previous studies have shown that SCZ risk genes regulate these processes. We obtained mNSCs from the subventricular zone (SVZ) of mouse brains at E14.5 and validated their identity using three well-characterized markers, SOX2, PAX6, and NESTIN. To mimic the effect of RERE upregulation on neurodevelopment, we overexpressed RERE in mNSCs. Proliferation assays showed that RERE overexpression inhibited the proliferation capacity of mNSCs. Furthermore, cell-cycle analysis revealed a significant increase in the proportion of cells in the G2/M-phase in the RERE-overexpression group compared with the controls, indicating that RERE-overexpression induced cell-cycle arrest at the G2/M-phase.

We also investigated the effect of RERE-overexpression on the differentiation of mNSCs. We used markers for astrocytes (GFAP), mature neurons (MAP2), oligodendrocytes (CLDN11), and immature neurons (TUBB3). After three days of spontaneous differentiation, the protein levels of GFAP and MAP2 were measured using IF, and the expression levels of Gfap, Map2, Cldn11, and Tubb3 were assessed using qPCR. The proportion of GFAP-positive cells did not differ significantly between the RERE-overexpression and control groups, indicating that overexpression of RERE did not affect astrocytic differentiation of mNSCs. However, the proportion of MAP2-positive cells was significantly reduced in the RERE-overexpression group compared with controls, indicating that RERE-overexpression inhibited neurogenesis. Consistent with IF results, qPCR analysis also revealed that Map2 and Tubb3 expression were significantly downregulated in the RERE-overexpression group compared with controls. By contrast, the expression of Gfap and Cldn11 was unchanged. Western blot results further confirmed that MAP2 protein levels were significantly reduced, whereas GFAP levels did not differ between the RERE-overexpression and control groups. Takentogether, these results indicate that RERE-overexpression impairs neural development by inhibiting the proliferation and differentiation of mNSCs.

RERE regulates pathways related to dendrite development and glutamatergic synapse
It has been reported that RERE acts as a nuclear receptor modulator to regulate the expression of specific genes. Moreover, RERE also regulates gene expression by acting as a coregulator of the retinoic acid (RA) signaling pathway. To elucidate the biological processes and signaling pathways regulated by RERE, we conducted transcriptome sequencing using RERE-overexpressing and control mNSCs. A total of 213 genes showed differential expression (|log2(FoldChange)|>1 and P-adj<0.05) in RERE-overexpressing and control mNSCs. Among them, 118 genes were downregulated, and 95 were upregulated. Several differentially expressed genes are related to neurodevelopment. For instance, Tnn is associated with neuronal development, Sema5a is involved in neurodevelopment and axonal projection, and has been linked to autism risk, and Erbb4, an important SCZ risk gene, is involved in central nervous system development and synaptic transmission. We validated the RNA-seq results with qPCR. The qPCR results of four selected genes (Erbb4, Sema5a, Fbln2, and Mest were selected as they exhibited highly significant P-values, i.e., ranked among the top 20%) and were consistent with RNA-seq, indicating the reliability of the transcriptomic analysis. Intriguingly, KEGG analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes were predominantly enriched in glutamatergic, cholinergic, and GABAergic synapses, three important neurotransmitter systems that have been reported to be involved in SCZ. GO analysis showed that the differentially expressed genes were enriched in pathways related to endomembrane system organization, vesicle organization, dendrite development, and related processes. These results suggest that RERE plays an important role in regulating pathways related to dendrite development and neurotransmitter systems.

Overexpression of RERE affects the density of dendritic spines and dendritic complexity
Dendritic spine alterations have been widely reported in SCZ. Accumulating evidence supports the dendritic spine pathology of SCZ. For example, one study showed that excessive pruning of dendritic spines in late childhood or adolescence may contribute to SCZ risk. Our previous studies also showed that dysregulation of the SCZ risk genes NAGA and NMRAL1 led to altered dendritic spine density. These findings suggest that risk genes may contribute to SCZ risk by affecting dendritic spines. Consistent with these observations, our RNA-seq analysis also suggested that RERE may have a pivotal role in dendritic spine morphogenesis. Differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in pathways related to dendrite development, GABAergic, glutamatergic, and cholinergic synapses. We thus investigated whether RERE has a role in regulating dendritic complexity and dendritic spine density. Dendritic complexity analysis showed that RERE-overexpression resulted in a significant increase in the number of neurites in rat cortical neurons. Dendritic spine density analysis further revealed that the densities of thin spines and the total spines were significantly reduced in RERE-overexpressing neurons compared with controls. In addition, compared with controls, the proportion of stubby spines was significantly increased in RERE-overexpressing neurons, while the proportions of other spine types (including long thin, filopodia, and branched spines) were significantly reduced. These results demonstrate the important role of RERE in regulating and maintaining dendritic spine density and complexity.

RERE regulates GluN2A
Transcriptome analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes between RERE-overexpressing and control mNSCs were significantly enriched in glutamatergic and GABAergic synapses. Additionally, dysfunction of glutamatergic receptors has been widely reported in SCZ. To further explore whether RERE contributes to SCZ by affecting the glutamatergic system, we conducted western blots and qPCR analyses. The expression of NMDA receptors (NMDARs) and AMPA receptors (AMPARs) was quantified. The results revealed a significant decrease in the expression of NMDAR subunits (Grin1, Grin2a, and Grin2b) and AMPAR subunits (Gria2). We further examined the expression levels of GABAergic subunits (Gaba-br2 and Gabrg2), the dopaminergic receptor Drd2, and Synaptophysin. The results showed that the RERE-overexpression significantly upregulated Gaba-br2 and Gabrg2, while Synaptophysin expression was significantly downregulated. In contrast, Drd2 expression remained unchanged. Western blot further revealed that GluN2A (encoded by Grin2a) was significantly reduced. GluN2B expression also showed a trend toward a decrease; however, this change did not reach statistical significance. Moreover, the levels of GluA4, GluK1, and PSD95 did not show significant variations, but synaptophysin expression was increased. Taken together, these results indicate that RERE regulates GluN2A, an important subunit of NMDARs, suggesting that RERE may confer SCZ risk by modulating the glutamatergic system.

RERE modulates NMDAR-mediated miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs)
Given the significant downregulation of GluN2A observed upon RERE-overexpression, we performed whole-cell recordings to examine NMDAR-mediated mEPSCs in primary rat frontal cortical neurons. mEPSCs offer a refined approach to study synaptic mechanisms, as each event reflects the quantal release of neurotransmitters and activation of receptors at individual synapses. At a holding potential of -70 mV, mEPSCs are mainly mediated by AMPARs because NMDARs are blocked by Mg²⁺. To relieve the voltage-dependent block of NMDARs, we used an Mg²⁺-free extracellular solution. We recorded NMDAR-mediated mEPSCs from rat frontal cortex neurons at -70 mV, in the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX, blocking action potentials), bicuculline (blocking inhibitory inputs), and 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX, blocking AMPA/kainate currents). Quantitative analysis revealed that RERE-overexpression reduced peak amplitude of NMDAR-mEPSCs by 16% (to ~84% of control values), suggesting impaired synaptic efficacy and reduced functional receptor density. Conversely, no significant alteration was observed in event frequency between groups, indicating that presynaptic glutamate release remains unaffected. Cumulative probability analysis demonstrated a pronounced leftward shift in amplitude distribution for RERE-overexpressing neurons, indicating an increased proportion of small-amplitude synaptic events. Collectively, these electrophysiological findings demonstrate that RERE-overexpression impairs NMDAR-dependent synaptic transmission, which correlates mechanistically with the observed GluN2A subunit depletion.

RERE-RXRA/RARB complex regulates Grin2a via promoter binding
To investigate how RERE-overexpression in neurons leads to the downregulation of Grin2a, we first performed TF binding predictions to explore if the promoter region (~2000 bp upstream of the transcription start site, TSS) of Grin2a contains binding sites for RERE-related TFs. This analysis revealed the presence of motifs for RARB and RXRA. Within this region, we identified two fragments, designated F1 and F2, both of which contained putative binding motifs for RARB and RXRA. RERE has been reported to function as a nuclear receptor modulator that interacts with the RAR/RXR heterodimer to regulate gene expression through retinoic acid response elements (RAREs). We therefore hypothesized that RERE represses Grin2a expression via this pathway. To test this, we first performed a dual-luciferase reporter assay and found that both F1 and F2 were transcriptionally active. However, their regulatory activity was attenuated upon RERE-overexpression, suggesting that RERE acts as a repressor. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments further demonstrated that RERE interacted with RXRA and RARB in rat neurons. To confirm the direct binding of RARB and RXRA to these promoter fragments, we performed Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR, which verified their enrichment at fragments F1 and F2. Finally, knocking down Rxra or Rarb in rat neurons resulted in a significant downregulation of Grin2a expression. Together, these findings indicate that RERE interacts with RARB and RXRA at the promoter region of Grin2a to repress Grin2a expression.

## Methods

Statistical fine-mapping
To identify putative causal variants within the 1p36.23 locus, we conducted fine-mapping using three methods: SuSiE, CARMA, and FINEMAP. Summary statistics from populations of European ancestry (from the largest SCZ GWAS) were used as input. Genotype data of European individuals (i.e., reference panel) were extracted from the 1000 Genomes project, and the LD matrix was calculated using PLINK (v.1.9). For SuSiE, we performed fine-mapping using the functions susie_rss() implemented in the R package susieR (v.0.14.2). For CARMA, we calculated the Z score and conducted fine-mapping using the R package CARMA (v.1.0). For the FINEMAP method, we utilized FINEMAP software (v1.4.2) to perform fine-mapping by using the Z file, LD file, and master file.

Colocalization analysis
To explore whether the same variants drive the expression of RERE and SCZ risk at the 1p36.23 locus, we conducted a colocalization analysis. The eQTL dataset was obtained from BrainMeta, which was constructed by using RNA-seq data of 2865 brain cortex samples. The SCZ GWAS dataset was obtained from Dang et al. We extracted the cis-eQTL of RERE in the 1p36.23 locus and the GWAS summary statistics of SCZ, and performed Bayesian colocalization analysis utilizing the R package coloc (v.5.2.3) with default parameters.

Investigation of the regulatory effects of rs159961 and rs301792 on RERE
To investigate whether rs159961 and rs301792 regulate RERE independently or synergistically, we performed both conditional eQTL and haplotype analyses. For conditional eQTL analyses, we applied the linear regression model implemented in R (lm() function) using the genotype and expression data from CMC, in which RERE expression was regressed on each SNP's allele either individually or jointly, thereby evaluating whether the effect of one SNP remained significant after conditioning on the other. We then phased the genotypes of rs159961 and rs301792 using Eagle2 to infer haplotypes and construct diplotypes for each individual, which resulted in a total of seven distinct diplotypes. To assess the impact of these diplotypes on RERE expression, we conducted linear regression analyses with diplotype groups included as categorical predictors. Setting individuals carrying the non-risk alleles at both SNPs on both chromatids (AC/AC) as the reference group, and subsequently estimating the association of RERE expression for each diplotype relative to this reference.

Transcriptome-wide association study
To translate the findings of SCZ GWAS into potential causal genes, we performed a TWAS to identify genes whose genetically regulated expression levels were associated with SCZ risk. Specifically, we integrated gene expression weights from the PsychENCODE project with SCZ GWAS summary statistics using FUSION software under default settings. The expression weights in the PsychENCODE dataset (N=1321) were calculated from genotype data and gene expression data with covariates adjusted. Further details are available in the original PsychENCODE publication and on the PsychENCODE website. For TWAS results, only genes that pass the Bonferroni-corrected P threshold (0.05/12434=4.02×10⁻⁶) are considered as TWAS significant genes.

Differential expression analysis
To identify differentially expressed genes between SCZ patients and controls, we utilized differential expression results from the PsychENCODE project, which quantified gene expression in postmortem human brain tissues. In brief, PsychENCODE collected RNA-seq data from postmortem human brains of SCZ patients and non-psychiatric controls across eight studies. They conducted strict quality control on all samples, discarding those with an ambiguous diagnosis, age, sex, or fewer than 10 million total reads. Outlier samples were also removed. After rigorous quality control, a total of 1442 high-quality RNA-seq data sets were obtained (including 899 non-psychiatric controls and 543 SCZ patients), and all samples were from the frontal or temporal cortex. In differential gene expression analysis, the authors considered the impact of all potential covariates on the results (including age, sex, and sequencing platform, among others) and incorporated these covariates into the differential gene expression analysis model. Finally, they identified 4821 genes that showed differential expression (FDR < 0.05) in SCZ cases and controls. More details on sample collection, expression quantification, and quality control can be found in the original article and on Synapse (doi.org/10.7303/syn12026837.1). The normalized expression values of RERE in SCZ cases and controls were downloaded from the PsychENCODE website, and visualizations were generated using ggplot2 in R (v4.1.1).

Cell culture
HEK-293T, SH-SY5Y, and U251 cell lines were purchased from the cell bank of Kunming Institute of Zoology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. B104 cells were purchased from Procell, Wuhan, China. HEK-293T, U251, and B104 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle medium (DMEM) (Gibco, C11995500BT), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco, 10091148) and 100 units/mL penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, 15140-122). SH-SY5Y cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, C12430500BT) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1mM sodium pyruvate solution (Gibco, 11360070), 1× MEM non-essential amino acids solution (Gibco, 11140050), and 100 units/mL Penicillin-Streptomycin. All the cells were cultured at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. PCR-based detection was conducted periodically to ensure that there was no mycoplasma contamination in the cultured cells.

Plasmid construction and generation of engineered cells
The full-length human RERE coding sequence (ENST00000377464.5) was cloned into the pCDH vector containing a 3×FLAG tag and GFP reporter. All constructs were verified by Sanger sequencing. For mNSCs, RERE overexpression was achieved by lentiviral transduction, followed by puromycin selection to establish stable overexpression prior to downstream experiments. Primary neurons used for assessing RERE overexpression efficiency and synapse-associated protein expression were transduced with lentivirus. For other neuronal experiments, RERE overexpression was achieved by transient transfection. RERE-overexpressing B104 cells were generated by lentiviral transduction and selected with puromycin to obtain stable cell populations before subsequent analyses. Other plasmids and engineered cell lines used in this study are described in detail in the corresponding Methods sections below. Plasmids were obtained from commercial sources or collaborators, where indicated.

Dual-luciferase reporter gene assays
Dual-luciferase reporter gene assays were performed as previously described. As the two functional variants are not located in the promoter region, we assessed their enhancer activity. DNA sequences (about 600 bp) containing the functional variants were cloned into the pGL3-Promoter vector (Promega, E1761). HEK-293T, SH-SY5Y, and U251 cells were seeded in 96-well plates at densities of 3.5×10⁴, 1×10⁵, and 3×10⁴ cells per well, respectively. After 24 h of plating, 100 ng of recombinant vector and 20 ng of the pRL-TK vector (internal control; Promega, E2241) were transfected into HEK-293T cells. For SH-SY5Y and U251 cells, 150 ng of recombinant vector and 30 ng pRL-TK vector were transfected using the Lipofectamine™ 3000 transfection reagent (Invitrogen, L3000-015). Twenty-four hours post-transfection, the Dual-Luciferase® Reporter 1000 Assay System (Promega, E1980) was used to quantify luciferase activity in HEK-293T cells. For SH-SY5Y and U251 cells, luciferase activity was measured 48 h post-transfection. Luminoskan Ascent chemiluminescence analyzer (Thermo Scientific, Thermo Luminoskan Ascent) was used to detect fluorescence activity. All sequences were validated by Sanger sequencing, and primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

To assess the activity of the Grin2a promoter region, two predicted motif-containing fragments, F1 and F2 (±500 bp around the putative RXRA and RARB binding motifs), were cloned into the pGL3-Promoter vector. These vectors were transfected into B104 cells, as well as B104 cells overexpressing RERE, and luciferase activity was measured 48 h post-transfection. The sequences of the promoter region of Grin2a, F1, and F2, are shown in Supplementary Fig. 10.

EMSAs
EMSAs were carried out as previously described. The EMSA Probe Biotin Labeling Kit (Beyotime, GS008) was used to label the synthesized oligonucleotide strands. The labeled oligonucleotides were then annealed. The nuclear extracts from SH-SY5Y cells were prepared using the Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Protein Extraction Kit (Beyotime, P0028). EMSA experiments were performed using the Chemiluminescent EMSA Kit (Beyotime, GS009). Nuclear proteins were first incubated without labeled probes for 10 min, then labeled probes were added, and the mixture was incubated for 20 min before electrophoresis. For super-shift experiments, the nucleoprotein was incubated with the corresponding TF antibody and unlabeled probes for 10 min, followed by the addition of labeled probes and incubation for 20 min. The sequences of all oligonucleotides are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

eQTL analysis
In order to explore whether rs159961 and rs301792 were associated with gene expression in the human brain, we examined their association with gene expression in three brain eQTL datasets, including the Common Mind Consortium (CMC), the Lieber Institute for Brain Development (LIBD), and BrainMeta v2. Briefly, the CMC dataset contains eQTL data from brain tissues of 467 post-mortem human brain samples, the LIBD dataset includes eQTL data from brain tissues of 412 post-mortem human brain samples, and the BrainMeta v2 dataset integrates brain sample genotype and RNA-seq data from seven cohorts (N=2443). Detailed information on sample collection, data processing, and eQTL generation can be found in the original studies.

CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing
CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing was used to knockout the segments containing the rs159961 and rs301792. Two sgRNAs (located upstream and downstream of the target SNP) were designed using the tool developed by the Zhang lab (https://zlab.bio/guide-design-resources). The sgRNAs were ligated into the pX459 vector (provided by Mr Yan Ruiqing), and the recombinant vector (3 μg) was transfected into SH-SY5Y (cultured in a 6-well plate) using the Lipofectamine™ 3000. The transfected cells were selected using puromycin (1 μg/mL), and puromycin-resistant cells were seeded into a 10 cm dish at a very low density for monoclonal growth. After several days of culture, monoclones were selected and plated onto 48-well plates. The knockout efficiency of each single clone was determined by PCR. The sequences of sgRNAs are listed in Supplementary Table 6, and the primer information for knockout efficiency verification is listed in Supplementary Table 7.

Real-time qPCR
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen, 10296028CN). Following the manufacturer’s protocol, 1 μg total RNA was reverse transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA) using the PrimeScript™ RT reagent Kit (Takara, RR047A). The expression of the target gene was determined using TB Green® Premix Ex Taq™ II (Tli RNaseH Plus) (Takara, RR820A). ACTB (for human) or Actb (for mouse or rat) was used as the internal control, and the results were analyzed using the 2−ΔΔCt method. All qPCR experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates, each measured in three technical replicates. qPCR was carried out using a CFX96 or CFX Opus 96 Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad), with data acquisition performed using Bio-Rad CFX Maestro and Bio-Rad CFX Manager software. qPCR primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Data 8.

Knockdown assays
The shRNAs were designed using the online tool at https://rnaidesigner.thermofisher.com and were cloned into the pLKO.1-EGFP-Puro vector (from XIAMEN Anti-hela Biological Technology Trade Company) or the pSicoR-Ef1a-mCh-puro vector (Addgene, 31845). The lentiviral packaging plasmids psPAX2, pMD2.G, and the constructed vector were co-transfected into HEK-293T cells (cultured in a 10 cm dish) using polyethyleneimine (PEI). Forty-eight hours post-transfection, the packaged viral particles were collected through a 0.22 μm filter and were used to infect SH-SY5Y cells or rat primary cortical neurons (cultured in a 6-well plate). qPCR was used to determine the expression levels of REST, POLR2A, RERE, Rxra, Rarb, and Grin2a. All shRNA sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 8.

Isolation and characterization of mNSCs
Isolation and characterization of mNSCs were performed as previously described in refs. 24–29. Briefly, the brains of embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) both male and female mice (C57BL/6J) were dissected, and tissues from the subventricular zone (SVZ) were obtained. The tissues were placed into pre-cooled proliferation medium (DMEM/F-12, Gibco, C11330500BT; 1× N2, Gibco, 17502048; 1× B27, Gibco, 12587010; basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) (20 ng/mL), STEMCELL, 78003; epidermal growth factor (EGF) (20 ng/mL), STEMCELL, 78006; and heparin, STEMCELL, 7980) and were dissociated with a 1 mL pipette (by repeated pipetting). The resultant cells were filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer and transferred into a fresh proliferation medium. After culturing for 2–3 days, neurospheres were selected and plated onto culture dishes (pre-coated with laminin, 3 μg/mL, Sigma, L2020-1mg). The identity of the isolated mNSCs was characterized with three neural stem cell markers, including SOX2 (R&D Systems, AF2018), PAX6 (Merck, AB2237), and NESTIN (Merck, MAB353).

Fluorescent-activated cell sorting
The 1.0×10⁶ mNSCs were plated onto 6-well plates, which were pre-coated with laminin (3 μg/mL). After culturing for 48 h, the mNSCs were harvested using StemPro Accutase (Gibco, A1110501). The dissociated cells were collected into a 15 mL centrifuge tube and centrifuged at 1000×g for 3 min at 4°C. The cell precipitation was gently rinsed with precooled phosphate buffer saline (PBS). The cells were then resuspended in 1 mL precooled PBS, and 3 mL absolute ethanol was added dropwise to achieve a final concentration of 75% ethanol. The mixture was thoroughly mixed and incubated at a temperature of 4°C for 24 h. The cell precipitation was collected by centrifugation at 1000×g for 5 min at 4°C and rinsed with precooled PBS. The cells were resuspended in 500 μL of propidium iodide (Beyotime, C1052) and incubated for 30 min at 37°C, shielding the samples from light. Red fluorescence was detected using a flow cytometer (BD, LSR Fortessa™), and the cell cycle was analyzed with FlowJo software version 10.8.1.

Proliferation of mNSCs
Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) and 5-Ethynyl-2’-deoxyuridine (EdU) assays were carried out as previously described. In brief, for the CCK-8 assay, 1×10⁴ cells were plated onto 96-well plates (pre-coated with laminin, 3 μg/mL). After culturing for 0, 24, 48, and 72 h, the absorbance at 450 nm was measured to estimate the cell viability. For the EdU assay, 2×10⁵ cells were plated onto 24-well plates (pre-coated with laminin, 3 μg/mL). After culturing for 48 h, 20 μM EdU (RIBO-Bio, C00054) was added into the medium and incubated for 45 min at 37°C (to label proliferating cells). EdU assays were conducted with the Cell-Light™ EdU Apollo 567 In Vitro Kit (RIBO-Bio, C10310-1) to detect EdU-labeled cells. Images were captured with a laser scanning confocal microscope (OLYMPUS, FV1000). Image analysis was performed using ImageJ software on three independent biological replicates, with five images acquired for each replicate.

Differentiation of mNSCs
Differentiation assays were performed as previously described. Briefly, 2×10⁵ cells and 1×10⁶ cells were plated onto 24-well and 6-well plates (pre-coated with laminin, 3 μg/mL), respectively. After culturing for 24 h in proliferation medium, the medium was replaced with differentiation medium (proliferation medium without bFGF and EGF). After differentiating for 3 days, cells were fixed for immunofluorescence (IF) staining. GFAP (Sigma, G9269) and MAP2 (Merck, AB5622) antibodies were used to label the astrocytes and neurons, respectively. Images were captured with a laser scanning confocal microscope (OLYMPUS, FV1000), with a total of 15 images obtained from three biological replicates. ImageJ software was used to count the GFAP-positive and MAP2-positive cells. qPCR was performed to detect the expression levels of Gfap, Map2, Tubb3, and Cldn11.

Western blot
Western Blot was carried out to determine protein expression levels. Cells were lysed in cold RIPA Lysis Buffer (Beyotime, P0013B) supplemented with PMSF (Beyotime, ST507) for 30-60 min. Homogenates were centrifuged at 12,000×g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected. After the protein concentration was determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime, P0010S), protein samples were mixed with loading buffer and heated in a dry bath heater at 95°C for 5-10 min. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. The membranes were blocked for 2 h at room temperature in 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST). Subsequently, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C in primary antibody dilution prepared with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in TBST. After washing the membrane with TBST six times (5 min each), the membrane was incubated for 1 h at room temperature in HRP-conjugated secondary antibody diluent prepared with 5% BSA in TBST. ECL substrate was used to detect the immunoblot signals. Protein band intensity was quantified using ImageJ software.

IF staining
After removing the medium and rinsing with PBS, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) (the mNSCs and the rat primary cortical neurons were fixed with 4% PFA containing 4% sucrose) for 15 min. Following three 5-min rinsing sessions in PBS, the cells were permeabilized with PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 (PBST) for 20 min. Next, the cells were blocked using the Immunol Staining Blocking Buffer (Beyotime, P0102) for 1 h at room temperature. Following this, the primary antibody was diluted in PBST containing 2% BSA and incubated at 4°C overnight. After several rinses with PBS, the cells were further incubated with the fluorescent secondary antibody (diluted in PBST containing 2% BSA) for 1 h at room temperature. Subsequently, the samples were mounted and imaged under a fluorescence microscope.

Transcriptome analysis
Differential expression analysis between RERE-overexpressed mNSCs and the control group was conducted following the widely used RNA-seq analysis pipeline. RNA sequencing was performed by Novogene Co. Ltd. After adapter trimming and filtering out low-quality reads, FastQC v0.11.9 was used to further confirm the high quality of reads. Clean reads were aligned to the grcm38 reference genome (downloaded from: https://cloud.biohpc.swmed.edu/index.php/s/grcm38_tran/) using HISAT2 v2.2.1. The SAM files were then sorted and converted to BAM format using SAMtools v1.9. Subsequently, StringTie v2.1.7 and PrepDE.py scripts were utilized for gene-level reads assembly and expression quantification. After filtering low-expressed genes (only genes with >10 counts in more than four samples were retained), differential expression analysis was performed on the quantified count matrix using DESeq2 v1.42.0. Genes with |Log2 FoldChange|>1 and a Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method adjusted P-value < 0.05 were considered to be differentially expressed.

Isolation of the rats' primary cortical neurons
The brains of embryonic day 17.5–18.5 (E17.5–18.5) Sprague Dawley rats (both males and females) were dissected, and tissues from the frontal cortex were isolated. The tissues were cut into small pieces and rinsed with pre-cooled Hank’s Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) (Gibco, 14175079) supplemented with 1% HEPES (Solarbio, H8090-100g) and 200 units/mL of penicillin-streptomycin. They were then digested in a pre-prepared digestion solution (Neurobasal, Gibco, 21103049; 2% B27, Gibco, 17504044; 1% GlutaMAX, Gibco, 35050061; 2 mg/mL Papain, Worthington, LS003119; 5 units/mL DNase I, Sigma, D4263) at 37°C for 20 min. The digestion was quenched with 5 mL of neuronal medium containing FBS (Neurobasal; 2% B27; 1% GlutaMAX; 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin; 2.5% FBS, Gibco, 10091148). The digested tissues were transferred to a 15 mL centrifuge tube, and the supernatant was aspirated after standing for 30 s. The remaining digested tissues were resuspended with 1.5 mL FBS-containing neuronal medium and slowly pipetted with the pre-sterilized pasteurized tube 8–9 times. After pipetting, the suspension was allowed to stand for 2–3 min to permit the undigested tissue mass to settle. The supernatant cell suspension was filtered through a 70 μm strainer and plated onto pre-coated 6-well plates. After 6-8 h of plating, half of the medium was aspirated from each well, and FBS-free neuronal medium (Neurobasal, 2% B27, 1% GlutaMAX) was added. The neurons were cultured for about two weeks, and the medium was changed every three days.

Analysis of the density and morphology of dendritic spines
After culturing the isolated rat primary neurons for 14–15 days, 3 μg pCDH-RERE-3×flag vector and 1 μg Venus plasmid (expressing GFP) were co-transfected into rat cortical neurons using Lipofectamine™ 3000. Three days post-transfection, IF staining was performed. The dendritic spines of neurons were captured with a laser scanning confocal microscope (ZEISS 880). NeuronStudio and ImageJ were used to analyze the density and morphology of neuronal dendritic spines.

Analysis of the complexity of neuronal dendrites
The isolated rat primary neurons were cultured for 3–4 days, then a co-transfection was performed using Lipofectamine™ 3000 to transfect 3 μg pCDH-RERE-3× flag vector and 1 μg Venus plasmid (expressing GFP) into rat cortical neurons. Neuronal morphology was captured using a ZEISS 880 confocal microscope, and the complexity of neurons was assessed using ImageJ software by Sholl analysis.

Electrophysiological recordings
Recordings were obtained using an EPC10 patch clamp (HEKA). The data were digitized at 10 kHz. The holding potential of primary rat frontal cortex neurons was set at −70 mV, and series resistance compensation was adjusted to 60–80%. Recordings with series resistances >20 MΩ or the leak current (Ileak) > −200 pA were rejected. The cells were recorded in an extracellular solution containing 140 mM NaCl (Sigma, S3014), 5 mM KCl (Sigma, P9541), 2.5 mM CaCl2 (Sigma, C7902), 10 mM HEPES (Sigma, H4034), and 10 mM D-glucose (Sigma, D9434) at pH 7.4 and 315 Osm. Electrodes with a resistance of 3–5 MΩ were pulled from borosilicate glass capillaries (WPI). The intracellular solution contained 120 mM K-Gluconate (MCE, HY-Y0569C), 5 mM NaCl (Sigma, S3014), 1 mM MgCl2 (Sigma, M2670), 0.2 mM EGTA (Sigma, E43T8), 2 mM MgATP (Sigma, A9187), 0.1 mM Na2GTP (Sigma, G8877), 10 mM HEPES (Sigma, H4034), and 10 mM phosphocreatine disodium (Sigma, HY-D0885B), adjusted to pH 7.2. When recording NMDAR-mEPSCs, 1 µM TTX (Hellobio, HB1034), 10 mM bicuculline (MCE, HY-N0219), and 10 µM CNQX (MCE, HY-15066) were added to the extracellular solution. Primary rat frontal cortex neurons from embryonic day 17.5–18.5 (E17.5–18.5) Sprague-Dawley rats were cultured on poly-D-lysine-coated (Sigma, P6407) glass coverslips and maintained at 37°C in the presence of 5% CO2 for 16–18 days before the experiment. Cells were transfected with 3 µg of plasmid per well in six-well plates, and electrophysiological recordings were performed 48–72 h after transfection. Data were analyzed using Clampfit 9.02 (Molecular Devices), Igor Pro 6.0 (WaveMetrics), and Prism 8 (GraphPad Software). Cumulative probability plots of NMDAR-mEPSC were plotted in Origin 2021. The normality of data distribution was assessed using the D’Agostino-Pearson omnibus normality test. Statistical differences were evaluated using the two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test, with a significance threshold set at P < 0.05.

Co-IP
We performed Co-IP using the Immunoprecipitation Kit with Protein A+G Magnetic Beads (Beyotime, P2179). Primary neurons from the rat prefrontal cortex were collected and lysed in lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors. After complete lysis, the samples were centrifuged at 10,000–14,000×g for 3–5 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected for subsequent immunoprecipitation assays. The RERE antibody (Bioss, bs-7077R) was diluted in 1× TBS and incubated with pre-washed Protein A+G magnetic beads on a rotator at room temperature for 15 min to 1 h. After washing the beads three times with 1× TBS, the collected protein lysates were added to the antibody-conjugated Protein A+G beads and incubated overnight at 4°C on a rotator. Following incubation, the supernatant was discarded, and the beads were washed three times with 1× TBS. The bound proteins were eluted by adding 100 μL of 1× SDS-PAGE Sample Loading Buffer, followed by heating at 95°C for 5 min. Finally, the samples were separated on a magnetic rack for 10 s, and the supernatant was collected for Western blot.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR
We performed ChIP experiments using the SimpleChIP® Enzymatic Chromatin IP Kit (CST, 9003) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Primary rat prefrontal cortical neurons were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 min, followed by quenching with glycine solution for 5 min at room temperature. After removing the supernatant, cells were washed twice with ice-cold PBS and collected in ice-cold PBS containing protease inhibitors. The cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 2000×g for 5 min at 4°C for subsequent experiments. Chromatin was digested with micrococcal nuclease and incubated at 37°C for 20 min. Cross-linked chromatin fragments were then incubated overnight at 4°C with the indicated antibodies, including IgG, RXRA (CST, 3085S), and RARB (Abcam, ab53161). For each IP reaction, 30 µL of ChIP-grade protein G magnetic beads were added and incubated for 2 h at 4°C. Enriched chromatin complexes were recovered by magnetic separation and washing, and the binding of RXRA and RARB was assessed by RT-qPCR. qPCR primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 9.

### Reviewer 2

This paper, "Functional variants at 1p36.23 confer risk of schizophrenia through modulating RERE," investigates how specific genetic variations contribute to schizophrenia (SCZ) risk by affecting the RERE gene. The study characterizes previously identified functional variants, rs159961 and rs301792, located in the intronic regions of the RERE gene at the 1p36.23 risk locus. These variants exhibit allele-specific enhancer activity. The risk alleles of both variants lead to higher enhancer activity, which is associated with increased RERE expression in human brain tissues. The risk allele of rs159961 reduces the binding of the transcription factor REST. The risk allele of rs301792 increases the binding of POLR2A. Both mechanisms result in stronger enhancer activity that subsequently regulates RERE expression. The study concludes that the functional variants rs159961 and rs301792 contribute to schizophrenia risk by upregulating RERE. This upregulation, in turn, affects neurogenesis, dendritic spine density, and synaptic transmission, thereby increasing SCZ risk. These findings provide a framework for translating GWAS findings into an understanding of disease biology and offer insights into SCZ pathogenesis. While the paper is comprehensive, it is fairly difficult to follow- especially how new versus reanalyzed data are presented is not made clear in the results or figure legend text. The methods are also lacking and critical experiments (e.g. possible synergistic effects of the two alleles) are noticeably missing.

Major comments
1. Very little detail provided in the TWAS section of the results. Only RERE is identified on the Manhattan plot- were other genes significant as well?
2. No details on the case control RNAseq/ microarray data? The authors cite several studies from which postmortem brain transcriptomics was used but do not provide a description of their overall analysis schema.
3. Are genes examined in Fig 5 from the overexpression experiment? Why are they not included in the validation figures? There also doesn’t appear to be any tables with the RERE OE transcriptomic data. This needs to be included.
4. For that matter, I could not find any additional data tables even though genomic data was generated (more below).
5. The variants rs159961 and rs301792 exhibit allele-specific enhancer activity. Both variants lead to higher enhancer activity, which is associated with increased RERE expression in human brain tissues. However, further investigation into whether rs159961 and rs301792 regulate RERE independently or synergistically are not performed. While the authors acknowledge this, the study is predicated on understanding both alleles so why these experiments were not performed is puzzling.
6. Elucidation of the exact regulatory mechanisms by which RERE affects the glutamatergic system. Is this a direct or indirect interaction? For example, RERE may bind to promoters of other genes that in turn regulate the observed genes. While the authors acknowledge this limitation, there is also no data table of the affected genes in the overexpression of RERE experiment which may help resolve this issue.
7. Can the authors speculate about the possibility of rs159961 and rs301792 regulating additional genes? There appears to be a high degree of chromatin looping in this area and other genes may be impacted.

Minor comments
8. There are many grammatical mistakes and awkward sentence transitions that will need to be addressed.
9. Lines 409-10 are not accurate. The data show that the introns containing rs159961 and rs301792 are enriched for the motif for REST and POLR2. Not that they affect the binding.
10. EMSA is not defined.
11. Sentence starting in line 469-472 doesn’t make sense. May need to be edited.
12. Lines 517-518 is not true. The data shows an effect of the SNPs on RERE expression but not specifically on SCZ.

### Reviewer 3

The study by Liu et al aims to characterise functional variants underpinning a schizophrenia genome-wide significant common variant locus at 1p36.23, and provide insights into how these variants impact schizophrenia pathophysiology. The paper presents a series of functional genomics experiments that implicate two functional variants (rs159961 and rs301792) at this locus. TWAS, eQTL and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments suggest these variants are associated with increased expression of RERE. Mouse neural stem cells (mNSCs) models suggest overexpression of RERE impairs proliferation of NSCs and neurogenesis, and also abnormalities in dendrite complexity and dendritic spine density. A transcriptomic analysis of RERE overexpressing NSCs identified 213 differentially expressed genes that were enriched for those with functions related to glutamatergic, cholinergic, and GABAergic synapse. Western blot and qPCR analyses also found RERE overexpression resulted in a decreased expression of the NMDAR subunit GRIN2A, which has been consistently been implicated in schizophrenia by common and rare genetic studies.

The manuscript is well written, and although a large number of analyses and results are presented the paper is easy to follow. The findings provide novel insights into the schizophrenia pathophysiological mechanisms associated with common risk alleles at 1p36.23. Since my background is in psychiatric genetics, my review specifically focusses on the TWAS, eQTL and differential gene expression elements of the paper. I have the following comments regarding these analyses.

1. The authors claim their findings support the neurodevelopmental hypothesis of schizophrenia, but I did not see any data from the eQTL or TWAS analysis implicating REME in early neuronal development. The authors show in Supplementary figure 5 that REME is expressed prenatally, but are the eQTL/TWAS analyses based on postmortem adult brain tissue? Since published schizophrenia TWAS based on human fetal brain did not find any significant associations with REME (PMID: 32366953, Supplementary Table 2), could the authors please clarify whether their eQTL/TWAS findings implicate specific development timepoints in schizophrenia, and if not comment on the conflicting TWAS findings for REME reported in Hall et al 2021 (PMID: 32366953).
2. The transcriptomic analysis identified 213 differentially expressed genes in RERE overexpressed mNSCs, but I did not see outputs of these experiments presented anywhere other than in Figure 5b. It would be helpful if the full results for each gene were presented as supplementary data, as it is not easy to identify which specific genes are differentially expressed from the figure. For example, I could not determine whether GRIN2A was differentially expressed from the figure. This comment is also relevant for any other analyses in the paper where results are only presented in figures; the raw results should also be available in table format where applicable.
3. In the transcriptomic analysis, genes with adjusted P-value <0.05 were considered differentially expressed genes. I could not see what method was used to adjust P values, could the authors please clarify?
4. The discussion opens by stating the "Neurodevelopmental hypothesis SCZ posits that SCZ is caused by a combination of environmental and genetic factors”. I think this sentence should end by saying that these factors impact brain development.
5. In the largest schizophrenia GWAS to date, RERE was prioritised through fine-mapping as the credible causal gene underlying 1p36.23 (main text and supplementary Table 12 in Trubetskoy et al 2022, PMID: 35396580). Given its relevance to the current study, I would suggest the authors cite this finding in the introduction and discussion.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To address the regulatory
mechanisms by which RERE affects the glutamatergic system, we performed additional serial
experiments in the revised manuscript. Specifically, we conducted transcription factor binding
prediction, reporter gene assays, Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), Chromatin
immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR, and transcription factor knockdown assays. To investigate
whether RERE regulates Grin2a directly or indirectly, we first performed transcription factor
binding predictions to explore if the promoter region ( ~2000 bp upstream of the transcription
start site, TSS) of Grin2a contains binding sites for RERE-related transcription factors. This
analysis revealed the presence of binding motifs for RARB and RXRA (Fig. 8a, b; Supplementary
Fig. 9). Within the promoter region, we identified two fragments, designated F1 and F2, both of
8
which contained putative binding motifs for RARB and RXRA (Supplementary Fig. 9). Of note,
RERE has been reported to function as a nuclear receptor modulator that interacts with the
RAR/RXR heterodimer to regulate gene expression through retinoic acid response elements
(RAREs)(16). We therefore hypothesized that RERE may repress Grin2a expression via this
pathway. We thus performed a dual-luciferase reporter gene assay. The results validated the
regulatory activity of both F1 and F2 fragments (Fig. 8c). We found that the regulatory activity of
F1 and F2 was attenuated upon RERE-overexpression (Fig. 8d; Supplementary Fig. 10), suggesting
that RERE acts as a repressor. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further demonstrated that
RERE interacted with RXRA and RARB in rat neurons (Fig. 8e). To confirm the direct binding of
RARB and RXRA to these promoter fragments, we performed ChIP-qPCR, which verified
enrichment of RARB and RXRA at fragments F1 and F2 (Fig. 8f, g). Finally, Rxra or Rarb knockdown
in rat neurons resulted in a significant downregulation of Grin2a (Fig. 8h-k). Taken together, these
results indicate that RERE interacts with RARB and RXRA to repress Grin2a expression directly
(Fig. 8l). The detailed results are presented in Fig. 8; Supplementary Fig. 9-10; page 15, lines 375-
387; page 16, lines 388-397; page 25, lines 634-638; page 26, lines 639; page 33, lines 866-879;
page 34, lines 880-896; and page 49, lines 1223-1236.

be impacted.

considered the possibility that rs159961 and rs301792 may regulate additional genes. We
therefore performed relevant experiments and analysis to investigate this. Our eQTL analysis
demonstrated that both variants are associated with the expression levels of RERE (P = 1.39 ×
10⁻⁴⁸ and P = 1.98 × 10⁻⁴⁹), RERE-AS1 (P = 4.56 × 10⁻⁸ and P = 4.72 × 10⁻⁸), and SLC45A1 (P = 1.51
× 10⁻⁴ and P = 1.64 × 10⁻⁴) (Fig. 2a), suggesting that these two variants may contribute
schizophrenia risk by modulating expression of these three genes. Furthermore, in CRISPR/Cas9-
mediated genome editing experiments, deletion of the genomic regions encompassing rs159961
and rs301792 resulted in a significant downregulation of RERE expression (Fig. 2f–j). Notably,
deletion of the rs159961-containing region also led to a marked reduction in SLC45A1 expression,
whereas deletion of the rs301792-containing region did not cause significant changes in SLC45A1
expression (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). RERE-AS1, a long noncoding RNA that modulates the
expression of nearby genes, was not assayed for expression changes. These results suggest that
rs159961 may influence the expression of both RERE and SLC45A1, whereas rs301792
predominantly affects RERE. Although rs301792 and rs159961 may also regulate SLC45A1,
the
eQTL results showed that the association significance between these two SNPs and RERE is
several orders of magnitude higher than SLC45A1, indicating RERE is the major target gene of
these two functional SNPs. We have revised the manuscript. Page 8, lines 155-157; page 8, lines

Response: We appreciate the reviewer for pointing this out. Specifically, rs159961, rs301792, and
RERE are located within the 1p36.23 region, an important risk locus for SCZ(4,11,17-19). These two
functional variants showed associations with SCZ in East Asians, with stronger association
significance observed in Europeans (Supplementary Fig. 1). Our eQTL analysis suggested that
functional risk variants confer SCZ risk by upregulating RERE, as the risk alleles of rs159961 and
rs301792 were associated with higher expression of RERE (Fig. 2a-e). This regulatory effect was
experimentally confirmed through dual-luciferase reporter gene assays and CRISPR-Cas9-

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
The study by Liu et al aims to characterise functional variants underpinning a schizophrenia
genome-wide significant common variant locus at 1p36.23, and provide insights into how these
variants impact schizophrenia pathophysiology. The paper presents a series of functional genomics
experiments that implicate two functional variants (rs159961 and rs301792) at this locus. TWAS,
eQTL and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout experiments suggest these variants are associated with increased
expression of RERE. Mouse neural stem cells (mNSCs) models suggest overexpression of RERE
impairs proliferation of NSCs and neurogenesis, and also abnormalities in dendrite complexity and
dendritic spine density. A transcriptomic analysis of RERE overexpressing NSCs identified 213
differentially expressed genes that were enriched for those with functions related to glutamatergic,
cholinergic, and GABAergic synapse. Western blot and qPCR analyses also found RERE
overexpression resulted in a decreased expression of the NMDAR subunit GRIN2A, which has been
consistently been implicated in schizophrenia by common and rare genetic studies.
The manuscript is well written, and although a large number of analyses and results are presented
the paper is easy to follow. The findings provide novel insights into the schizophrenia
pathophysiological mechanisms associated with common risk alleles at 1p36.23. Since my
background is in psychiatric genetics, my review specifically focusses on the TWAS, eQTL and
differential gene expression elements of the paper. I have the following comments regarding these
analyses.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments on our work. We also
greatly thank the reviewer for these insightful comments and suggestions. Our point-by-point
responses are provided below.
1. The authors claim their findings support the neurodevelopmental hypothesis of schizophrenia,
but I did not see any data from the eQTL or TWAS analysis implicating REME in early neuronal
development. The authors show in Supplementary figure 5 that REME is expressed prenatally, but
are the eQTL/TWAS analyses based on postmortem adult brain tissue? Since published
schizophrenia TWAS based on human fetal brain did not find any significant associations with REME
(PMID: 32366953, Supplementary Table 2), could the authors please clarify whether their
eQTL/TWAS findings implicate specific development timepoints in schizophrenia, and if not
comment on the conflicting TWAS findings for REME reported in Hall et al 2021 (PMID: 32366953)
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In this study, the eQTL/TWAS
analyses were based on postmortem tissues from the adult brain. To specifically address the
reviewer’s concern, we performed additional analyses using prenatal brain data.
expression in prenatal brain samples from Walker et al.(20). No significant eQTL associations were
detected (rs159961: beta = 0.044, P = 0.596, FDR = 1; rs301792: beta = 0.134, P = 0.117, FDR = 1).
The lack of significant findings may be explained by the small sample size in the prenatal dataset
(N = 201) compared with postnatal datasets (N > 400)(21,22), which limits statistical power for eQTL
discovery. Moreover, gene expression during early brain development undergoes greater
dynamic changes and may be subject to more complex genetic regulatory mechanisms(13,20),
further complicating the detection of robust eQTL effects between rs159961/rs301792 and RERE
expression.
We next attempted to perform TWAS analysis using prenatal brain data. Following the same
approach as Hall et al.(23), we applied the FUSION pipeline to generate expression weights from
fetal brain RNA-sequencing and genotype data to predict cis-regulated transcript levels. However,
the cis-heritability of RERE expression in the prenatal dataset was very low (h2=-0.002, P=0.498),
which precluded the training of reliable TWAS weights. By contrast, the adult brain dataset
exhibited sufficient heritability (h2 = 0.084, P = 1.925×10-3), thereby enabling robust TWAS
modeling.
We also carefully reviewed the study by Hall et al.(23). Their fetal brain TWAS was based on
120 prenatal samples, in which they reported only 1,351 genes and 3,985 transcripts with
sufficient heritability for TWAS. Importantly, RERE was not included in the gene-level dataset,
and only a single RERE transcript was analyzed at the isoform level. The limited number of genes
and transcripts identified in this study, coupled with the small sample size and low genetic
heritability, may explain why RERE was not significantly associated with SCZ.
In summary, while current prenatal brain datasets are underpowered to reliably assess RERE
and SCZ associations, our integrative analyses in adult brain tissues, together with findings from
large-scale genetic studies(4,11) and our complementary wet-lab cellular experiments, support the
hypothesis that RERE plays a role in neurodevelopmental processes relevant to SCZ. We have
added this clarification and discussion of the fetal TWAS study to the revised manuscript. Page
8, lines 159-161; page 9, lines 211-212; page 10, lines 213; page 18, lines 456; page 19, lines 457-
467.
